summary: Engadget's Jessica Conditt reviews the Steam Deck OLED, a mid-cycle refresh of Valve's handheld rather than a Steam Deck 2. It brings an HDR OLED screen, a more efficient die-shrunk AMD APU, better battery life, thermals, haptics and Wi-Fi, while keeping the same large form factor. She scores it 89 and calls it a welcome improvement on an already good device.
one_line: Engadget scores the Steam Deck OLED 89, praising its HDR screen, battery life and thermals while noting the handheld is still very large.
key_facts: The Steam Deck OLED is a mid-cycle refresh from Valve, not the Steam Deck 2, and Engadget gave it a score of 89.
The OLED screen is 7.4 inches (versus 7 inches on the original) with smaller bezels, native HDR, a wider P3 color gamut and a peak brightness of 1,000 nits versus 400 nits originally.
The display has no variable refresh rate (VRR) support but tops out at 90Hz, compared with 60Hz on the original.
Valve claims the battery lasts 30 to 50 percent longer and charges from 20 percent to 80 percent in 45 minutes.
The device uses a die-shrunk version of the custom AMD APU with the same CPU and GPU, so developers keep the same performance targets; it weighs about 30 grams less than the original.

Size is unchanged at 11.7 inches long, 4.5 inches tall and nearly 2 inches thick, and the thumbsticks are 1mm taller; the reviewer, who has smaller-than-average hands, still finds it huge but less top-heavy.
In a Hades test at 800p with a 60 fps cap, the OLED lasted four hours and 23 minutes versus two hours and 42 minutes for the original, a 62 percent improvement (the original is aging).
Playing Elden Ring maxed out, the OLED battery lasted two hours and 20 minutes, about 40 percent longer than the original.
Heat management is better: the larger fan is not louder and the palms do not sweat as with the original.
It has a Wi-Fi 6E module and Bluetooth 5.3 with a dedicated antenna; top download speed on a regular Wi-Fi 6 router was 562mbps, about 10 percent faster than the old model.
The Steam Deck OLED goes on sale November 16th at 1pm ET: the 512GB model costs $550, the 1TB model $650, and a limited edition 1TB model $680.
Valve keeps selling the 256GB LCD model at a reduced $400, and will sell through backstock of the 64GB and 512GB LCD models.
More than 10,000 Steam titles are labeled playable or verified, out of four labels: unknown, unsupported, playable and verified.
Valve developers call the HDR OLED model the definitive version of the Steam Deck, what they would have released in 2022 had the technology existed.
